title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Princess Shtcherbatskaya thought it was out of the question for the wedding to take place before Lent, only five weeks off, since not half the trousseau could possibly be ready in time. But she had to agree with Levin that putting it off until after Lent would be cutting it too late: an old aunt of Prince Shtcherbatsky's was seriously ill and might die, in which case mourning would push the wedding back even further. And so, deciding to split the trousseau into two parts — a larger one and a smaller one — the princess agreed to a wedding before Lent. She determined to have the smaller part of the trousseau ready now and the larger part made later, and she was very annoyed with Levin because he couldn't give her a serious answer to whether he approved of this arrangement or not. The arrangement suited all the better because, right after the wedding, the young couple were to leave for the country, where the more important part of the trousseau would not be needed.

Levin remained in the same dazed state, in which it seemed to him that he and his happiness were the chief and only goal of all existence, and that he no longer needed to think about anything or worry about anything — everything was being done and would be done for him by others. He had no plans or aims for the future; he left it to others to arrange, knowing that everything would turn out wonderfully. His brother Sergey Ivanovitch, Stepan Arkadyevitch, and the princess guided him in what he had to do. All he did was agree with whatever was suggested. His brother raised money for him, the princess advised him to leave Moscow after the wedding, Stepan Arkadyevitch advised him to go abroad. He agreed to everything. "Do whatever you like, if it amuses you. I'm happy, and my happiness can't be any greater or any less for anything you do," he thought. When he told Kitty about Stepan Arkadyevitch's idea of going abroad, he was greatly surprised that she didn't agree to it and had quite definite preferences of her own about their future. She knew that Levin had work he loved in the country. She did not, as he could see, understand that work, and she didn't even care to understand it. But that didn't keep her from regarding it as very important. And then she knew that their home would be in the country, and she wanted to go there — not abroad, where she wasn't going to live, but to the place where their home would be. This clearly stated preference astonished Levin. But since he didn't care either way, he immediately asked Stepan Arkadyevitch — almost as if it were his obligation — to go down to the country and arrange everything there as well as he could, with that taste of his that he had so much of.
"By the way," Stepan Arkadyevitch said to him one day after coming back from the country, where he had got everything ready for the young couple's arrival, "do you have a certificate of confession?"
"No. Why?"
"You can't get married without one."
"_Aïe, aïe, aïe!_" cried Levin. "It must be nine years since I've taken the sacrament! I never thought of it."
"You're a fine one!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, laughing. "And you call me a Nihilist! But this won't do, you know. You have to take the sacrament."
"When? Only four days are left now."

Stepan Arkadyevitch arranged this too, and Levin had to go to confession. For Levin, as for any unbeliever who respects other people's beliefs, taking part in any church ceremony was extremely disagreeable. At this moment, in his softened state, sensitive to everything, this inevitable act of hypocrisy was not merely painful to Levin — it seemed impossible. Now, in the height of his glory, his fullest flowering, he would have to be either a liar or a mocker. He felt incapable of being either. But although he repeatedly pestered Stepan Arkadyevitch about the possibility of getting a certificate without actually taking communion, Stepan Arkadyevitch insisted that there was no way around it.
"Besides, what does it cost you — two days? And he's a very nice, clever old fellow. He'll pull the tooth out for you so gently you won't even notice."
Standing through the first litany, Levin tried to bring back in himself his youthful memories of the intense religious feeling he had gone through between the ages of sixteen and seventeen.

But he was instantly convinced that this was completely impossible for him. He tried to look at it all as an empty custom with no meaning, like the custom of paying social calls. But he felt he couldn't do that either. Levin found himself, like most of his contemporaries, in the vaguest position with regard to religion. He couldn't believe, and at the same time he had no firm conviction that it was all wrong. And so, unable to believe in the importance of what he was doing, and unable to look on it indifferently as an empty formality, throughout the whole preparation for the sacrament he felt uncomfortable and ashamed at doing what he didn't himself understand — what, as an inner voice told him, was therefore false and wrong.

During the service he would first listen to the prayers, trying to attach some meaning to them that wasn't at odds with his own views; then, feeling he couldn't understand them and would have to condemn them, he tried not to listen and to attend instead to the thoughts, observations, and memories that drifted through his mind with extreme vividness during this idle stretch of standing in church.

He had stood through the litany, the evening service, and the midnight service, and the next day he got up earlier than usual and, without taking tea, went to the church at eight in the morning for the morning service and his confession.

There was no one in the church except a beggar soldier, two old women, and the church staff. A young deacon, his long back showing in two distinct halves through his thin undercassock, met him and, going at once to a little table by the wall, read the exhortation. During the reading, especially at the frequent rapid repetition of the words "Lord, have mercy on us!" which rang back from the echo, Levin felt that his thoughts were shut and sealed away, and that they mustn't be touched or disturbed now, or chaos would follow. So, standing behind the deacon, he went on thinking about his own affairs, neither listening to nor examining what was being said. "It's wonderful what expression there is in her hand," he thought, remembering how they had been sitting at a corner table the day before. They had nothing to talk about, as was almost always the case at this point, and laying her hand on the table she had kept opening and shutting it, laughing as she watched her own movement. He remembered how he had kissed it and then traced the lines on her pink palm. "Have mercy on us again!" Levin thought, crossing himself, bowing, and watching the supple flex of the deacon's back as he bowed in front of him. "She took my hand then and traced the lines. 'You have a splendid hand,' she said." And he looked at his own hand and at the deacon's short one. "Yes, it'll be over soon," he thought. "No, it seems to be starting again," he thought, listening to the prayers. "No, it's just ending — there he is bowing to the ground. That's always the end."

The deacon's hand in its plush cuff unobtrusively accepted a three-rouble note, and he said he would enter it in the register; then, his new boots creaking jauntily across the flagstones of the empty church, he went off to the altar. A moment later he peeped out from behind it and beckoned to Levin. Thoughts, until then locked up, began to stir in Levin's head, but he hurried to push them away. "It'll come out right somehow," he thought, and walked toward the altar rails. He climbed the steps and, turning to the right, saw the priest. The priest, a small old man with a thin grizzled beard and tired, kindly eyes, was standing at the altar rails turning the pages of a missal. With a slight bow to Levin he began at once to read prayers in the formal voice. When he had finished them, he bowed to the ground and turned to face Levin.

"Christ is present here unseen, receiving your confession," he said, pointing to the crucifix. "Do you believe in all the doctrines of the Holy Apostolic Church?" the priest went on, looking away from Levin's face and folding his hands under his stole.
"I have doubted, I doubt everything," Levin said in a voice that grated on himself, and he stopped.
The priest waited a few seconds to see if he would add anything, then, closing his eyes, he said rapidly, with a broad Vladimir accent:
"Doubt is natural to the weakness of mankind, but we must pray that God in His mercy will strengthen us. What are your particular sins?" he added without a pause, as though anxious not to lose time.
"My chief sin is doubt. I have doubts about everything, and most of the time I'm in doubt."
"Doubt is natural to the weakness of mankind," the priest repeated, using the same words. "What is it you doubt most of all?"

"I doubt everything. I sometimes even have doubts about the existence of God," Levin couldn't help saying, and he was horrified at the impropriety of his own words. But Levin's words didn't seem to make much impression on the priest.
"What sort of doubt can there be of the existence of God?" he said quickly, with a barely perceptible smile.
Levin said nothing.

"How can you doubt the Creator when you look at His creation?" the priest went on in his rapid customary patter. "Who has decked the heavens with their lights? Who has clothed the earth in its beauty? How explain it without a Creator?" he said, looking inquiringly at Levin.
Levin felt it would be improper to get into a metaphysical discussion with the priest, so he confined himself to a direct answer to the question.
"I don't know," he said.
"You don't know! Then how can you doubt that God created everything?" the priest said, with good-humored bewilderment.
"I don't understand any of it," Levin said, blushing, feeling that his words were silly and could only be silly in such a setting.

"Pray to God and ask Him. Even the holy fathers had doubts and prayed to God to strengthen their faith. The devil has great power, and we must resist him. Pray to God, beseech Him. Pray to God," he repeated hurriedly.
The priest paused for a while, as if thinking.
"You're about, I hear, to marry the daughter of my parishioner and son in the spirit, Prince Shtcherbatsky?" he resumed, with a smile. "A fine young lady."
"Yes," Levin answered, blushing for the priest. "What does he want to ask me about that at confession for?" he thought.
And as if in answer to his thought, the priest said:

"You are about to enter into holy matrimony, and God may bless you with children. Well — what sort of upbringing can you give your little ones if you don't overcome the temptation of the devil that draws you into unbelief?" he said, with gentle reproach. "If you love your child like a good father, you won't only want wealth, luxury, and honor for your baby; you'll be anxious for his salvation, for his spiritual enlightenment by the light of truth. Yes? What answer will you give him when the innocent child asks you: 'Papa! Who made everything that enchants me in this world — the earth, the waters, the sun, the flowers, the grasses?' Can you say to him: 'I don't know'? You cannot but know, since the Lord God in His infinite mercy has revealed it to us. Or your child will ask you: 'What awaits me in the life beyond the tomb?' What will you say to him when you know nothing? Will you leave him to the temptations of the world and the devil? That isn't right," he said, and stopped, putting his head on one side and looking at Levin with his kind, gentle eyes.

Levin made no answer this time — not because he didn't want to argue with the priest, but because, up to now, no one had ever put such questions to him, and when his children did, there would be time enough then to think about how to answer them.

"You are entering a stage of life," the priest continued, "where you must choose your path and stick to it. Pray to God, that He in His mercy may help you and have mercy on you!" he concluded. "Our Lord and God Jesus Christ, in the abundance and riches of His loving-kindness, forgives this child…." And, finishing the prayer of absolution, the priest blessed him and dismissed him.

Walking home that day, Levin had a wonderful sense of relief that the awkward business was over and that he had got through it without having to lie. Beyond that, there was a vague memory that what the kind, nice old fellow had said hadn't been nearly as stupid as he had thought at first, and that there was something in it that needed to be cleared up.

"Not now, of course," Levin thought, "but at some point later on." Levin felt more strongly than ever that there was something unclear and unclean in his soul, and that, with regard to religion, he was in the same position he could see so clearly and dislike so much in others, and for which he blamed his friend Sviazhsky.

Levin spent that evening with his betrothed at Dolly's, and was in very high spirits. To describe to Stepan Arkadyevitch the state of excitement he was in, he said he felt as happy as a dog being trained to jump through a hoop, who, having finally caught the idea and done what was asked of it, whines and wags its tail and leaps up onto tables and windows in its delight.
